title: Knowledge Check 3: Lessons 11-14
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 11-14 of the ai-power-user series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Priya's vendor summary ran to completion and the tool reported success, but the headline total was a few hundred dollars off because the tool pulled a stale version of one vendor's numbers. Per the lesson, what is this an example of?
options: A silent error, a failure where the system does not behave as expected but surfaces no visible error, alert, or warning, so the workflow reports success while the output is wrong
A hallucination, because the tool invented a number that did not exist
A mid-flow break, because the workflow stopped partway through the run
A dry run failure, because the tool refused to produce any output
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a silent error as a situation where a system fails to behave as expected but does not surface any visible error, alert, or warning. Priya's run reported success while the total was wrong, which is exactly that. A hallucination is a fabricated claim, not a stale number; a mid-flow break is a run that stops partway; and the tool did produce output, so it is not a dry run failure.

questions.question: Priya asked her tool to write about a new vendor, and it produced a confident paragraph with a citation to a case study that turned out not to exist. Per the lesson, what is the right way to describe what happened?
options: A hallucination, a response that presents fabricated information as fact, such as a citation to a source that does not exist, and the fix is to verify the specific claim against something real
A silent error, because the tool reported success without sending an alert
A mid-flow break, because the tool stopped before finishing the paragraph
A versioning error, because the prompt had not been saved as a new version
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a hallucination as a response that presents fabricated information as fact, and notes that a large language model may embed plausible-sounding falsehoods such as fabricated citations. Priya's invented case study is the signature example. It is not a silent error (no stale data), not a mid-flow break (the tool finished), and not a versioning issue.

questions.question: Priya's overnight run stopped partway: it pulled the data and drafted the report but never sent it. When she re-ran it, the second run picked up where it stopped instead of duplicating the draft. Per the lesson, what property made the re-run safe?
options: Idempotency, the property that a request can be retried with no additional side effects, so the result happens only once even if the call is made multiple times
A dry run, because the tool ran in a safe mode that produced no output
A silent error, because the tool failed without surfacing an alert
A hallucination, because the tool invented the draft on the second run
questions.explanation: The lesson defines an idempotent operation as one where a request can be retried with no additional side effects, so the result happens only once even if the call is made multiple times. Priya's re-run finished the job instead of doubling it, which is idempotency in action. A dry run produces no real output, a silent error is a wrong result, and a hallucination is a fabricated claim, none of which describes a safe re-run.

questions.question: Priya's monthly vendor summary feeds a procurement review the team holds on the first Tuesday of each month. Per the lesson, how should she set its cadence?
options: Run it the morning of the review, so the output is ready when the decision that uses it is actually made
Run it every hour so the data is always as fresh as possible
Run it the day after the review so this month's work is already complete
Run it twice a day so nobody ever has to wait for an update
questions.explanation: The lesson argues that the right cadence is not the fastest one but the one that matches when the output gets used. Priya's review is the decision that uses the data, so she schedules the run for the morning of it. Hourly or extra runs produce the same result more often without improving it, and running after the review misses the decision it feeds.

questions.question: Which choice best describes an event hook as the lesson defines it?
options: A workflow that starts when an event happens, such as a file being added to a folder, rather than waiting for a fixed clock time
A workflow that runs on a scheduled day and time whether or not anything changed
A way to make a workflow process several items together in a single run
A store where items wait in line when work arrives faster than it can be processed
questions.explanation: The lesson defines an event hook (a webhook) as starting a workflow on an event rather than on a clock: the other system notifies yours when the event occurs. A scheduled run on a fixed time is the opposite (clock-based), batching is processing items as a group, and a queue is the store that absorbs work arriving faster than it can be handled.

questions.question: In the lesson, what is a queue for, and why does it matter?
options: It lets extra work line up and be processed in order at a steady pace when input arrives faster than the workflow can handle it, so nothing gets dropped during a rush
It makes the workflow run more often so spikes never build up
It processes every new item the moment it arrives instead of waiting
It replaces the schedule so the workflow only ever runs on events
questions.explanation: The lesson describes a message queue as a line where items are added on one end and taken off the other in arrival order, letting the sender hand off work and the receiver process it at its own pace. During a spike it absorbs the difference so the workflow clears the backlog without dropping any items. Running more often, immediate processing, or event-only triggers do not describe the queue's role.

questions.question: Priya wants to add purchase recommendations with spend levels to her monthly vendor summary. Per the lesson, which step in her workflow should earn a review gate?
options: The data pull, because it is the foundation everything else builds on
Before a purchase recommendation becomes a suggestion, because the tool cannot see the context she holds (the pricing dispute, the pilot category) and a bad spend number is expensive to unwind
Every step in the workflow, so nothing can ever ship without a human
The formatting step, because a clean layout matters most to leadership
questions.explanation: The lesson has Priya run her workflow through the four triggers (irreversibility, low confidence, external visibility, context gaps) and gate only the steps that earn a pause. The recommendation step has low confidence as new, holds context the tool cannot see, and carries an expensive-to-unwind spend number, so it earns a gate before it becomes a suggestion. She deliberately does not gate the data pull, which is routine and reversible (it earns rhythm, not a pause), and gates, rather than leaves ungated, the customer-facing summary.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is the distinction between human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop?
options: Human-in-the-loop stops the workflow until a person approves the output before it proceeds, while human-on-the-loop lets the workflow execute and a person monitors and steps in after the fact
There is no practical difference; the terms are interchangeable
Human-in-the-loop monitors output from the side, while human-on-the-loop is a required approval step inside the flow
Human-in-the-loop is for low-risk steps and human-on-the-loop is for high-risk steps
questions.explanation: The lesson defines human-in-the-loop as a model where the human must review, approve, or act on the output before any automated system proceeds, with the human decision inside the path and judgment a required step. Human-on-the-loop is the opposite: the workflow executes within policy limits and a human monitors from the side, stepping in to intervene after the fact. Confusing them matters because they fail differently, and the second kind fails quietly.

questions.question: The lesson warns that automation complacency can undo a well-placed review gate. What does this failure look like, and what does the lesson say is the defense?
options: The tool runs out of memory and silently drops a step, and the defense is to add more storage
The workflow skips the gate entirely on its own, and the defense is to re-run the workflow more often

Humans over-trust the system once it has been reliable, rationalize anomalies, and stop questioning outputs, and the defense is to design the gate so a genuine check is the path of least resistance rather than an act of willpower
The gate slows the workflow so much that no one wants to use it, and the defense is to remove the gate
questions.explanation: The lesson describes automation complacency as humans over-trusting a system, rationalizing anomalies, and stopping questioning its outputs; the more reliable the system appears, the less vigilant its overseers become. Because reliability itself breeds the skimming, the defense is structure: a gate built into the flow that hands the reviewer the information needed to decide and cannot be skipped, making a real check the path of least resistance. The stage is not about the tool failing storage, skipping steps on its own, or being too slow to use.

questions.question: Dev's support-ticket prompt had drifted into a single wall of uncommented text. His manager reads the sections in a fixed order fix, and his weekly summary runs off the same prompt. Per the lesson, which habit is the one that makes the rest of the refactor possible?
options: Structure: dividing the prompt into labeled sections (role, audience, task, instructions, format, variable slot) with a consistent delimiter, so a reader can see which part does what
Making every instruction absolute so the model never has to interpret
Rewriting the whole prompt from scratch each week so it stays fresh
Removing the sections so the prompt reads as one continuous paragraph
questions.explanation: The lesson argues structure is the first habit because everything else depends on it: once the prompt is divided into labeled, delimited sections, you can tell the machine which text is a rule and which is data in, and you can read which part does what. Without structure there is no frame for maintainability or comments to live in.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what does a comment on a prompt rule record that the rule itself usually does not?
options: The why: the reason the rule exists, the incident or constraint that decided it, so a future reader knows whether the reason still holds before they touch the rule
A longer, more detailed restatement of the same instruction
A second copy of the rule in different words so the model sees it twice
Nothing; comments are only for the model, never for a human reader
questions.explanation: The lesson says a comment records why a rule exists, not just what it does, the reason that a future reader or a future you needs to know before editing. Restating the rule adds nothing, duplicating it couples the rules together, and the comments' second audience is a human reader, with the why-line also helping the model weigh the rule by intent.

questions.question: Dev knows the executive summary must stay one line and the section order must stay fixed. Per the lesson, what is the maintainability test that tells him the rules are coupled and need separating?
options: A change that should touch exactly one rule forces him to edit several: the same rule is stated in multiple places, or a variable inputs slot is woven into the instructions, so one edit risks silently breaking the rest
The prompt has more than one labeled section
The prompt output changes when the underlying tool gets an update
The prompt is longer than a page
questions.explanation: The lesson defines maintainability as the property that lets a single small edit change one rule without damaging the others except his change touches multiple spots, the rules are coupled: the same fact or constraint appears in scattered sentenceshare, and a variable slot is entangled with fixed instructions. That coupling is the warning sign. More sections are the cure, not the disease, and tool updates and raw length do not measure coupling.
